guide.title: Consent, Refusal & Advance Directives
guide.lead: Every touch needs consent. Adults with capacity decide for themselves, even when you disagree; unconscious patients in an emergency are treated under implied consent. When someone refuses, make sure the refusal is informed, capable and voluntary – and write it down.

sections.title: Types of consent
rows: A capable adult agrees after you explain what you'll do, why, and the risks – in words or by actions
Unconscious or unable to decide, with a serious threat: the law assumes they would agree
A parent or guardian decides. Emancipated minors (married, in the military, financially independent, or a parent) decide for themselves. Emergency with no parent: implied consent
Court order, emergency mental health hold or police custody, per local law

sections.title: Can this patient refuse?
sections.question: An adult (or emancipated minor) who can understand, retain and weigh the information and communicate a choice – not impaired by low oxygen, low glucose, head injury, intoxication or shock?
sections.yes: Respect the decision. Explain the risks (including death) in plain words, offer alternatives and a way back, involve family if they agree, call medical direction, document.
sections.no: They lack capacity for this decision: treat in their best interest under your protocol, with police and medical direction as needed.

steps.title: Assess
steps.text: Full assessment and vital signs if they allow; mental status and glucose.

steps.title: Inform
steps.text: What you think is wrong, what could happen, what treatment offers, other options.

steps.title: Persuade
steps.text: Try again, involve family or friends, and ask medical direction to speak to them.

steps.title: Leave a safety net
steps.text: Call back any time; signs that mean call now.

steps.title: Document
steps.text: Capacity, what you explained, their words, signature or refusal to sign, a witness.

sections.title: Advance directives
rows: No CPR if they arrest. Everything else is still offered.
A medical order for the level of treatment: full, limited or comfort; CPR, intubation, antibiotics, tube feeding
The patient's wishes, often vague ("no heroic measures"). Without a DNR or POLST: start care and call medical direction
A named person decides when the patient can't

sections.title: Rules of thumb
items: Not sure a document is valid or present? Start care and call medical direction
A DNR is not "do not treat"
A valid directive outweighs family wishes
Organ donor status never changes resuscitation
A patient on a legal mental health hold can't refuse transport

quiz.q: Unconscious, unidentified crash victim with head trauma. Which consent applies?
quiz.explanation: Serious threat and unable to decide.

quiz.q: Who can give consent for their own care?
options: A 15-year-old with a school trip form

quiz.q: A capable patient who agreed earlier now says 'stop'. You:
options: Stop and explain the risks of refusing
quiz.explanation: Consent can be withdrawn at any time.

quiz.q: A patient on a legal mental health hold:
options: Can't refuse transport for the evaluation
Must go to a medical hospital first
quiz.explanation: Still assess and treat medical problems.

quiz.q: 90-year-old in arrest; the nurse shows a valid out-of-hospital DNR. You:
options: Withhold CPR and give comfort care per protocol
Ask medical direction for permission to honour it

quiz.q: A capable man with chest pain refused, signed after being told he could die, and died 2 hours later. Most accurate?
options: A capable, informed, voluntary, documented refusal protects the crew
The crew can't be protected because he died
quiz.explanation: Capacity, information and documentation are the defence.

quiz.q: Living will says 'no heroic measures'; SpO₂ 82% in respiratory distress; no DNR or POLST. You:
options: Treat fully with oxygen and transport; contact medical direction
Follow the living will word for word
quiz.explanation: Oxygen isn't heroic, and a living will isn't a medical order.

quiz.q: Under organ donation law, you should:
options: Give all patients the same full resuscitation
Call the transplant service before treating
Take donors to a transplant centre
quiz.explanation: Donation is considered only after death.

quiz.q: Combative, psychotic patient on a police mental health hold refuses the stretcher. Your role:
options: Police handle safety and restraint; you assess, treat and transport under the hold
DNR covers CPR only; POLST also covers intubation, antibiotics and tube feeding
POLST is valid only in nursing homes
quiz.explanation: POLST is a broader medical order.

quiz.q: After a crash, an alert woman smelling of alcohol wants to sign out. You:
options: Assess capacity carefully – alcohol can impair it – and involve medical direction
Let her sign and note the alcohol
quiz.explanation: Intoxication doesn't always remove capacity, but you must check.

quiz.q: 92-year-old with dementia and possible sepsis; DNR says 'no CPR'; family wants her to die at home. You:
options: Explain options; comfort care and treatment of the sepsis are allowed – the DNR covers only CPR; follow her known wishes with medical direction
Leave immediately: she has a DNR
quiz.explanation: If a POLST or proxy chooses comfort care at home, palliative pathways may apply.

flashcards.question: Expressed vs implied consent
flashcards.answer: Expressed: a capable, informed adult agrees. Implied: unconscious or unable to decide in an emergency – the law assumes they would agree.

flashcards.question: A valid refusal
flashcards.answer: Capable (not impaired by hypoxia, glucose, head injury, intoxication or illness), informed of the risks, voluntary, and documented.

flashcards.question: Consent for minors
flashcards.answer: Parent, guardian or person in that role. Emancipated minors decide for themselves. Emergency with no parent: implied consent.

flashcards.question: POLST vs DNR
flashcards.answer: DNR: CPR only. POLST (or MOLST and similar): a medical order covering CPR, intubation, antibiotics, tube feeding and the overall level of care.

flashcards.question: Documenting a refusal
flashcards.answer: Assessment and vital signs, capacity, what you recommended, risks explained, their words, signature or refusal to sign, witness, medical direction contact.

flashcards.question: Mental health hold
flashcards.answer: A patient on a valid legal hold can't refuse transport for evaluation. Assess and treat medical problems; police manage safety.

flashcards.question: Treating regardless of ability to pay
flashcards.answer: Care can't be refused or delayed for insurance, money or status. In US hospitals, EMTALA requires screening and stabilisation for everyone.

flashcards.question: Healthcare power of attorney
flashcards.answer: The person the patient chose to decide for them when they can't. Follow their decisions within the law and your protocol.

critical.scenario: 68-year-old, pale and sweaty, 8/10 chest pain to the left arm for 45 minutes. BP 100/68, HR 104. 'I know it's a heart attack. I'm not going.' His son says he's not confused.
critical.question: How do you manage the refusal?

options.t: Check capacity carefully (perfusion, glucose, understanding), explain the risks plainly, keep persuading, involve medical direction; if he still refuses with capacity, document fully with witnesses
Have him sign and leave at once

options.f: He's conscious and may have capacity.
Refusing care isn't a mental illness.

critical.explanation: Leave aspirin per protocol and tell the family to call back immediately.
critical.kpi: Assesses capacity and manages a high-risk refusal

critical.scenario: 85-year-old with advanced dementia, glucose 42 then 38 mg/dL, increasingly drowsy. The daughter says a living will says 'no extraordinary measures'; nobody can find it. You have standing orders for glucagon.
critical.question: How do you proceed?

options.t: Treat the hypoglycaemia now (IM glucagon), explain that without a valid order you must give emergency care, and contact medical direction if she objects

options.f: No valid document, and glucose isn't extraordinary.
Not safe in a drowsy patient.

critical.explanation: Simple, reversible treatment fits almost anyone's wishes.
critical.kpi: Provides emergency care when an advance directive is unverified

critical.scenario: 2 a.m., a 19-year-old international student: slurred speech, unsteady, smells of alcohol; vital signs stable. She refuses: she fears losing her scholarship and visa.
critical.question: How do you handle the refusal?

options.t: Assess capacity; with slurred speech and ataxia she probably lacks it. Reassure her about confidentiality, contact medical direction, transport in her best interest, and document accurately
Let her sign: she explains herself well
options.f: Clear reasons don't prove capacity when intoxicated.

options.t: Leave the drinking out of the report
options.f: Never alter the record; confidentiality protects her instead.

critical.explanation: Hospitals don't report patients to universities; tell her so.
critical.kpi: Assesses capacity in an intoxicated patient and documents truthfully
